citation: The Chicago Democrat. Vol. I, No. 1. Chicago, Ill.: John Calhoun, Tuesday, November 26, 1833.
author: John Calhoun, editor and publisher
repository: Chicago Historical Society — the front page carries its ownership stamp at top right, and '51177' is pencilled in the bottom margin of the same page, an accession or call number. Supplied to this project by the project owner as page scans of a bound volume, 2026-08-10, with a modern transcription.
locator: THREE page images, and they are NOT in issue order: page2.jpg is the FRONT page (it carries the full masthead), page3.jpg is the EDITORIAL page, and page1.jpg is the ADVERTISEMENT page — its column 1 continues an article running down page3's last column, so it follows the editorial page. The paper states it is 'printed on an imperial sheet', i.e. FOUR pages; only three are in the scan set, so one page of a four-page first issue is very likely still unread. Cite the page image and the advertisement heading for every claim. The advertisement columns carry their own dates — Oct. 4, Nov. 7, 18, 22, 25 and 26, 1833 — which are the dates of the copy, not of the issue.
note:
THE FIRST CONTEMPORARY CHICAGO DOCUMENT IN THIS DATASET, and the first tier-1 textual source it holds. Everything else describing the town's buildings is retrospective: Andreas 1884 is tier 3 and fifty years after the fact, the chicagology pages are compilations, and Kinzie's Wau-Bun is a memoir of 1856. This is the town describing itself, in its own week, to its own readers — and an advertisement is a peculiarly good witness because the advertiser was paying for it and his customers had to be able to find him.

WHAT MAKES IT EVIDENCE ABOUT BUILDINGS AT ALL: a business advertisement fixes that a trade was being carried on in Chicago in November 1833, and sometimes fixes where. It does not establish what the building looked like, and it does not establish that the same building stood on 1835-07-01 — this issue is NINETEEN MONTHS before the scene date, in the town's fastest-changing period. Treat it as strong evidence of existence and address, weak evidence of survival, and no evidence at all of form.

VERIFIED BY READING THE SCAN DIRECTLY, 2026-08-10, not from the accompanying transcription. That distinction earned itself immediately: the transcription renders the dry-goods firm as 'C. & L. Harmon' where the scan plainly reads 'C. & I. HARMON'. The transcription is a useful finding aid and is NOT the source; every claim must be taken from the page image.

THE STRONGEST SINGLE ITEM is the paper's own imprint, which is self-reported and therefore about as good as an address gets: 'THE DEMOCRAT, Is published every Tuesday, in the village of Chicago, Cook co. Ill. in the building on the corner of South Water and Clark-streets.' Note precisely what that settles — the JUNCTION, not the corner. It says 'on the corner of', and which of the four corners is not in the sentence. Andreas's 'SW corner' remains a separate, later, weaker claim.

A TRAP THIS SOURCE CONTAINS: the 'Two Buildings to Let' advertisement carries an engraving of a three-storey building with regular fenestration. Nineteenth-century jobbing printers kept generic stock cuts for exactly these categories, and the same block would be struck for any property advertisement. It is NOT a picture of a Chicago building and no elevation, storey count or window arrangement may be taken from it. The same applies to the ox and the strayed-cattle cuts.

CORRECTIONS TO THIS RECORD, 2026-08-11, after a full column-by-column read at 2.4x-9x. The first is mine and is the kind that propagates silently.

1. THE TAVERN KEEPER'S PREDECESSOR IS 'Wm. W. WATTLES', NOT 'Wm. W. Barlow'. I wrote Barlow into this record from a first quick read; the line reads WATTLES at 8x and Barlow appears nowhere in the issue. A misreading inside a tier-1 source record is worse than a missing record, because everything downstream inherits it wearing the authority of the original. It had already been passed to a builder before it was caught.

2. A THIRD TRAP, and it is positioned to do real damage. In the RIGHT MARGIN of the advertisement page, level with the imprint, in a later hand, IN PENCIL, someone has written 'S. W.' — cursive, grey, outside the column rule, manifestly not letterpress. It is a later reader's gloss supplying 'south-west', and it was almost certainly written by somebody who had read Andreas. If it were ever transcribed as part of the page it would look like contemporary corroboration of the south-west corner and would silently promote `chicago_democrat_office.position` from inferred to documented on no evidence whatever. The 1833 TYPE says only 'on the corner of'. The corner is still not in this document. Quarantine the annotation exactly as the stock cuts are quarantined.

3. 'Daniel Elston & Co.' — the word after the ampersand is OBLITERATED BY AN INK BLOT and is not readable. 'Co.' is a reasonable expansion and is not a reading.

4. A NEGATIVE FINDING WORTH AS MUCH AS A POSITIVE ONE: there is no mention of an estray pen anywhere in this issue. The corporation's own November 1833 code legislates hogs at large in detail and says nothing about impounding; the taken-up notices are county-clerk estray filings from Du Page and Walker's Grove, not Chicago. Andreas's claim that the estray pen was Chicago's 'first public building' gets no contemporary corroboration here, and the project should say so before anything rests on it.

5. THE FRONT PAGE'S 'market house' IS SPRINGFIELD'S, credited '—Sangamo Journal.' Do not read a market house into 1833 Chicago from this issue.
access_notes: Scans held outside the published payload. Page 1 is 2984 x 3776 px greyscale; pages 2 and 3 are 2744 x 3672. The advertisement columns are legible at native resolution; the news columns are legible in part. A modern transcription of the issue accompanies the scans and is a finding aid only.
what_it_supplies: that a named trade was being carried on in Chicago in November 1833
the Chicago Democrat's own address, self-reported: the corner of South Water and Clark streets
Philo Carpenter advertising drugs, medicines, oils, paints and dye-stuffs, dated Nov. 22, 1833 — with NO address, so it cannot disambiguate his two shops
C. & I. Harmon advertising dry goods, crockery, hardware and wet and dry groceries, dated Nov. 18, 1833 — with NO address, so it does NOT corroborate the Clark/South Water corner Andreas gives them
W. Kimball's 'New Store' at the corner of South Water and Clark — a SECOND, independently attested occupant of that junction in the same issue, signed
Peter Cohen, clothier and grocer, self-reported at the EAST END OF SOUTH WATER-STREET, and trading in Chicago before Nov 1833 ('old customers ... past favors')
Goss & Cobb, saddle and harness makers, self-reported on the corner of Lake and Canal streets
Matthias Mason & Co., blacksmiths, on 'Main-street, nearly opposite Graves' Tavern' — a street name this project does not otherwise hold
B. Jones, grocery and provision store, and separately a storage/forwarding/commission business — both ads give NO street
Newberry & Dole, forwarding and commission merchants — no address
John Wright, cut nails and general merchandise; and TWO BUILDINGS TO LET until 1 June 1834
Daniel Elston & [illegible], soap and candle manufactory, paying cash for tallow and house ashes
a tavern stand kept by Chester Ingersoll, 'lately occupied by Mr. Wm. W. WATTLES', dated 4 October 1833
the house of Chester Ingersoll used as the district polling place, 9 December 1833
THE VILLAGE ORDINANCES of 7 November 1833, complete — the richest single item in the paper
Ordinance 1: the corporate limits surveyed ALONG the northern United States' Pier 'to the termination thereof' — the pier as an existing, walkable structure with a definite landward end
Ordinance 5: 'either of the bridges in said town' and their 'plank or any piece of timber' — EXACTLY TWO bridges on 7 Nov 1833, of plank-and-timber construction

Ordinance 6: wooden buildings with wooden and lath-and-plaster partitions, heated by STOVES not fireplaces, pipes passing through roof or side wall and carried 18 inches above the roof, guarded by stone-ware pipe, brick, tin or sheet iron
Ordinance 9: timber, stone, brick, boxes and barrels stacked in the streets
Ordinances 3, 7 and 8: hogs at large, horses run through the streets, stallions
the schooner Austerlitz, Capt. Smith, from Buffalo, arrived about the 1[9]th inst. with a full cargo of merchandise for citizens of this village and cleared on the 21st IN BALLAST
a school established in the village by Mr. Sproat of Boston, already running on 26 Nov 1833
a public auction of United States property held AT FORT DEARBORN, 2 December 1833
the village population passing 'more than eight hundred souls' in late 1833
what_it_does_not_supply: any building's form, material, storey count or fenestration
the specific corner of any junction it names — the imprint says 'on the corner of', and which of the four is not in the sentence

evidence that any building named here still stood on 1835-07-01 — this issue is NINETEEN MONTHS before the scene date, in the town's fastest-changing period, and the population went from 800 to 3,265 in between
any length or width for the piers
any corroboration of the estray pen — see the negative finding in the note
